metadata.title: Soup visual decision brief builder
metadata.subtitle: A reusable sequence for turning the Part II soup visuals into an executive pricing note.

workflow.label: Decision question
workflow.question: Should Progresso investigate whether its soup prices are countercyclical?
workflow.artifact: One sentence naming lever, outcome, unit, and time.
workflow.red_flag: The brief starts with a dashboard screenshot instead of a pricing question.

workflow.label: Evidence grain
workflow.question: What does one row mean in the soup evidence?
workflow.artifact: Store-month panel contract plus brand, region, and season fields.
workflow.red_flag: A seasonal pattern is discussed without saying whether rows are stores, months, or store-months.

workflow.label: Visual metrics
workflow.question: Which metrics carry the visual argument?
workflow.artifact: Volume, share, price, log volume, log price, and active-store coverage.
workflow.red_flag: The brief mixes price, share, and volume without units or baselines.

workflow.label: Comparisons
workflow.question: Which comparisons make the pattern visible?
workflow.artifact: Winter versus non-winter, Progresso versus Campbell, region facets, and January index.
workflow.red_flag: The dashboard uses a national average when the decision might differ by region.

workflow.label: Uncertainty and limits
workflow.question: Which caveats should sit next to the charts?
workflow.artifact: Store coverage, interval plots, descriptive trend labels, and causal limit statement.
workflow.red_flag: A smooth trend line is interpreted as a causal elasticity estimate.

workflow.label: Executive brief
workflow.question: What should the manager do after seeing the visuals?
workflow.artifact: One-page brief: pattern, evidence, limits, and next pricing test.
workflow.red_flag: The page ends with another chart instead of a decision or next analysis.

sections.label: Decision question
sections.memo_text: This brief asks whether Progresso should investigate a pricing policy that appears to raise price when seasonal soup demand is weak. The decision is not an immediate price cut; it is whether the pattern deserves a pricing test or deeper causal analysis.
sections.evidence_standard: Names the lever as price, the outcome as volume/share, the unit as store-month, and the season window as winter versus non-winter.
sections.limit: A broad statement about seasonality is not enough; the brief must name the possible managerial action.

sections.label: Evidence grain
sections.memo_text: The core evidence is a monthly store panel with brand-level volume and price. Each row is a store-month observation, enriched with region and season labels. Aggregated visuals are summaries of that panel, not separate datasets.
sections.evidence_standard: The brief states the row contract before presenting aggregate seasonal charts.
sections.limit: If row grain is hidden, store coverage changes can masquerade as demand changes.

sections.label: Visual metrics
sections.memo_text: The main descriptive metrics are Progresso volume, Progresso share of category volume, average price, log volume, log price, and active-store count. Indexed views use January as the baseline so price and demand can be read on one comparison scale.
sections.evidence_standard: Each chart labels units, baseline, and whether values are raw, shares, logs, or indexes.
sections.limit: A price index and a volume index should not be read as dollars or cases sold.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.memo_text: The visual sequence compares winter with non-winter, Progresso with Campbell, national patterns with regions, and raw distributions with log-transformed distributions. These comparisons convert the dashboard from inventory into an argument.
sections.evidence_standard: Every figure answers one named comparison and leads to the next comparison.
sections.limit: A single national average can hide a regional pricing problem or a regional opportunity.

sections.label: Uncertainty and limits
sections.memo_text: The interval plots show that some seasonal share comparisons are precise enough to guide attention, but precision is not causality. The log-price/log-volume slopes preview elasticity and must be labeled as descriptive.
sections.evidence_standard: The brief keeps coverage, uncertainty, and causal limits near the visuals they qualify.
sections.limit: A descriptive slope can be visually persuasive and still be confounded by seasonality, promotions, assortment, or competitor action.

sections.label: Executive brief
sections.memo_text: The proposed brief says: Progresso volume and share fall sharply outside winter while price rises; the pattern varies by region; descriptive slopes suggest a strong price-volume association; the next step is a pricing test or quasi-experimental design before changing national policy.
sections.evidence_standard: The recommendation separates observed facts, managerial concern, and the next credible test.
sections.limit: The visual brief can justify investigation. It cannot by itself estimate the profit-maximizing price.

rubric.why_it_matters: Students reuse one business setting while learning multiple chart forms.
The eye can see season, region, brand, and price-volume contrasts.
The dashboard does not turn descriptive evidence into causal proof.
The brief hands off naturally to pricing, regression, and causal chapters.
